// Figure 8.1 — File 1, Slide 7

Input-Output Model of Program Testing

Both validation and defect testing use the same fundamental I/O model.

I/O Testing Model — Validation & Defect Slide 7 · File 1

Figure 8.1: Test data (inputs) are fed into the system. Outputs are observed and compared against expected results. Match = validation pass. Mismatch = defect exposed.

// Figure 8.2 — File 1, Slide 11

Inspections vs Testing

Static vs Dynamic V&V — Complementary Techniques Slide 11 · File 1

Figure 8.2: Inspections (static) and Testing (dynamic) are complementary. Inspections cannot check non-functional properties. Testing cannot catch errors before code exists. Use both.

// Figure 8.3 — File 1, Slide 15

Software Testing Process Model

Stages: Unit → Integration → System → Acceptance Slide 15 · File 1

Figure 8.3: The four-stage testing pipeline. Each stage uses the output of the previous as input. Defects found late are more expensive to fix — test early and often.

// Figure — File 1, Slide 25

Automated Test Components

The 3-part structure every automated test must have.

Setup → Call → Assert structure (from slides) Slide 25 · File 1

Automated Test Structure: Every test (Jest, Pytest, JUnit) follows this 3-part pattern. The assertion is the "oracle" — it determines pass or fail automatically.

// Figures 8.5 & 8.6 — File 1, Slides 30–31

Equivalence Partitioning & Partition Ranges

Fig 8.5 — Partitioning Concept Slide 30
Fig 8.6 — Input: 4–10 integers > 10,000 Slide 31

Fig 8.5 & 8.6: Equivalence partitioning divides input space into valid/invalid classes. Test one value from each class. Always add boundary values (4, 10, 9999, 10000) as these are where bugs hide.

// Figure 8.7 — File 3, Slide 4

Interface Testing

Component A calls Component B — Interface Error Types Slide 4 · File 3

Figure 8.7: Interface testing verifies that components interact correctly. Errors cannot be found by unit testing — they only appear when components are used together. Test with extreme parameter values and stress message-passing systems.

// Figure 8.8 — File 3, Slides 11–12

Collect Weather Data Sequence Diagram

System Testing derived from Use Case Sequence Diagram Slides 11–12 · File 3

Figure 8.8: Use-case sequence diagrams drive system test cases. Each message arrow becomes a test case — verify the correct message is sent, received, and the correct data returned.

// Figure 8.9 — File 3, Slide 16

Test-Driven Development Cycle

TDD Process — Red → Green → Refactor Loop Slide 16 · File 3

Figure 8.9: TDD enforces the discipline: test first, code second. The loop repeats for every small increment of functionality. Benefits: 100% code coverage, built-in regression, simplified debugging, living documentation.

// Figure 8.11 — File 3, Slide 30

Acceptance Testing Process

6-Stage Acceptance Testing Process Slide 30 · File 3

Figure 8.11: Acceptance testing is a formal process. Rarely do all tests pass — negotiation between developer and customer is expected. The final stage is a formal accept/reject decision.

// File 2 — Slide 2 (Screen Clipping — Real Image)

Basis Path Testing Steps

4 Steps — extracted directly from slide Slide 2 · File 2

Basis Path Testing Steps: (1) Draw CFG, (2) Calculate Cyclomatic Complexity, (3) List all independent paths, (4) Design test cases from paths. These 4 steps are the exam-expected answer format.

// File 2 — Slide 3

CFG Symbols & CC Formula

Control Flow Graph Notation + CC = E – N + 2P Slide 3 · File 2

CFG Symbols: Nodes = blocks of statements. Edges = flow between blocks. Decision nodes create branching. CC tells you how many independent paths exist and therefore the minimum test cases needed.

// File 2 — Slide 16 (Hand-drawn Solution)

Example 4: Hand-drawn CFG Solution + CC=5

📖

Study this carefully: This is the instructor's own hand-drawn answer — the exact format expected in exams. Note: CC = E–N+2 = 21–18+2 = 5. The table shows 5 paths with for1, for2, if combinations.

Hand-drawn CFG + CC=5 + path table (real image from slide) Slide 16 · File 2

Key observations from this solution: (i) The nested loops (for1, for2) each create a decision node. (ii) CC = 21–18+2 = 5. (iii) The path table shows boolean T/F for each decision. (iv) The hand-drawn CFG shows how nested loops create a complex back-edge structure.
